newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ rejects introduction of rabbit-killing virus.
newsitem.headline: NZ rejects introduction of rabbit-killing virus.

text.p: The New Zealand government officials said on Wednesday it will not allow the importation of a rabbit-killing virus that is rife across the Tasman.
New Zealand farmers watched enviously as rabbit calicivirus disease (RCD) spread through Australia after escaping a quarantine trial in October 1995.
They clamoured for its release in New Zealand, arguing it offered a "once-in-a-lifetime chance" of beating the country's rabbit problem.
Rabbits infest over half of New Zealand's land area. They strip vegetation, erode soil through burrowing and have reduced some high country areas almost to moonscapes.
But after a year of discussion and submissions, the Ministry of Agriculture (MAF) rejected importing the virus, saying too little was known about it.

MAF deputy director-general Peter O'Hara said there was "significant uncertainty" over RCD's effectiveness in killing rabbits as its impact on Australian rabbit populations varied. It is not even known exactly how the disease is spread.
"I recognise that my decision will disappoint and even anger many people who are struggling to deal with rabbits using current technology," O'Hara said.
The Minister of Agriculture was one of those disappointed.
"Farmers in some areas are facing very high costs for rabbit control and I fully understand their frustration at the decision," minister Lockwood Smith said.

"I have instructed MAF to carry out an urgent investigation of how the virus is spread. I want our scientists working with Australian authorities to get answers to the questions raised by the report as soon as possible," he said.

But environmentalists who had vigorously opposed introduction of the virus, welcomed the decision. They had argued that it could spread to native fauna, even though extensive ministry testing concluded this would not happen

"It's a very wise decision which recognises the many uncertainties in terms of the introduction of RCD," said Eugenie Sage of the Royal Forest and Bird Protection Society. "We welcome the decision as one which recognises the substantial risks and uncertainties involved," she told Reuters.
Smith noted that O'Hara had not stated RCD should never be introduced, merely that it should not be introduced yet.
"I want to help see how we can make it effective for the future as part of a rabbit control strategy," Smith said.

Twenty million rabbits are estimated to have died within three months of the virus infecting Australian rabbit populations. In September 1996, RCD was officially approved for use there, and has now spread through all parts of Australia.
Rabbits infected with RCD die from respiratory and heart failure within 40 hours and with no visible distress.
RCD has killed hundreds of millions of wild rabbits on four continents since it was first seen in domestic rabbits in China in 1984. A vaccine now exists to protect domestic rabbits.
Sage said New Zealand's last experiment with biological control, the introduction of stoats and ferrets last century to control rabbits, had been a disaster for indigenous wildlife.
Ironically, she said if RCD had been introduced and rabbit numbers reduced, stoats and ferrets -- which prey on rabbits -- would switch to native birds, lizards and insects.
